Earnings Beat Could Be A Big Test For Nutanix Stock (NTNX)
Sasha Jovanovic
Wed, October 28, 2026 at 11:08 AM EDT 4 min read
NTNX
SMCI
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Nutanix recently paired strong Q2 results with new AI-focused alliances, including Supermicro and Netris, aimed at simplifying enterprise and neocloud AI infrastructure.

The mix of better-than-expected quarterly performance and concrete AI stack offerings positions Nutanix squarely in the thick of hybrid-cloud and VMware exit spending decisions.

We will look at how Nutanix's investment narrative is shaped by its stronger Q2 delivery and deeper AI infrastructure partnerships.

Spot 55 AI infrastructure stocks that, like Nutanix, are tied directly to real AI infrastructure spending and could be next in line for investor attention.

Nutanix Investment Narrative Recap

The big belief with Nutanix is that it can turn its hybrid cloud and AI platform into a long term subscription engine, even as more workloads move to public cloud providers. The short term story hinges on converting recent Q2 momentum and AI buzz into durable annual contract value, while keeping operating discipline tight after a very large earnings jump.

The biggest near term swing factor is how effectively Nutanix captures VMware exit and AI infrastructure projects without letting sales and R&D spending run ahead of demand. The main risk is that competition, pricing pressure, and any slowdown in customer expansion blunt net retention, which would make recent margin strength harder to sustain.

The Supermicro alliance around Nutanix Agentic AI is the clearest operational tie in to the current AI narrative. It packages Nutanix Cloud Platform, Supermicro servers, NVIDIA GPUs, Nutanix Unified Storage, and Kubernetes into a ready to deploy inference stack. That speaks directly to enterprise buyers that want private AI, but do not want to assemble dozens of vendors.

For catalysts, this kind of full stack offer gives Nutanix a way to compete for larger AI infrastructure budgets rather than just selling core HCI software. Execution risk is real. Nutanix still has to prove it can scale GPU ready clusters efficiently, manage support complexity with partners, and do all of that while keeping margins and operating expenses under control.

Nutanix Analyst Expectations in Context

Nutanix's narrative projects US$4.2b revenue and US$673.9m earnings by 2029. That implies 13.8% yearly revenue growth and an earnings decline of about US$826m from current earnings of US$1.5b.

Uncover why Nutanix's fair value indicates a 9% potential upside to its current price that could narrow quickly.

NasdaqGS:NTNX 1-Year Stock Price Chart
Exploring Other Perspectives

Some of the lowest Nutanix forecasts lean hard into a different risk. They worry that GPU capacity and complex neocloud rollouts slow AI deals, so ARR builds more slowly than headlines suggest. Those analysts were pencilling in about US$4.1b revenue and US$517.0m earnings by 2029, well below consensus. The new Supermicro and Netris alliances may eventually push them to revisit that story.

Dell Is Up 299% in 2026: Take Profits, or Buy More? ©Dean Drobot via Canva
Key Takeaways

Dell stock is up 299% in 2026, with sharp rallies after two earnings reports that brought record AI server orders and a $95 billion backlog.

The business has earned much of the run: Dell raised its full-year revenue outlook to $192 billion, up 69%.

Barclays argues that higher memory prices drive much of Dell's growth, but Super Micro's much stronger preliminary quarter suggests AI server demand is holding.

At 17x forward earnings, Dell is worth buying more only if its late-November report shows free cash flow catching up with profit.

Dell Technologies (DELL:NYSE) stock is up 299% in 2026 through Tuesday's close, and the business has done most of the lifting.

It's also 16% below its Sept. 18 high, after a downgrade questioned what's really behind that growth. So do you take profits here, or buy more?

Two Reports Built a $95 Billion Backlog

Dell's May 28 first-quarter report started it. Revenue jumped 88% to $43.8 billion, and management lifted its full-year revenue outlook to $165 billion to $169 billion, from $138 billion to $142 billion in February.

The Sept. 1 second-quarter report topped that:

Revenue up 58% to a record $47.0 billion

A record $60.9 billion of AI server orders

A record $95 billion AI backlog

Full-year revenue guidance raised by $25 billion to $192 billion, with AI server revenue now expected at $74 billion (up from $60 billion)

As CFO David Kennedy put it at Citi's conference on Sept. 10, "Demand was faster than the P&L."

Barclays Says It's Memory Prices

Wall Street now expects revenue to climb from $113.5 billion in the year ended January 2026 to $193 billion this fiscal year and $231 billion the year after.

DELL Revenue, Actuals and Estimates: Fiscal 2024-2029 (TIKR)

Barclays thinks a lot of that is memory. Analyst Tim Long downgraded Dell to Equal Weight on Oct. 14 and lowered his target to $574 (from $603). His case: there's no "meaningful AI inflection" in enterprise spending yet, and much of Dell's growth comes from passing higher memory costs on to customers. If those prices level off, Dell's sales could too.

Dell concedes part of that. Traditional server and networking revenue rose 122% to $10.5 billion last quarter, and COO Jeff Clarke said on the second-quarter call, "There's a notion of inflation inside our growth."

title: Super Micro Is Down 32% in a Year. Is It Time to Sell, or Load Up?

Super Micro Is Down 32% in a Year. Is It Time to Sell, or Load Up?
Rexielyn Diaz

SMCI
Trade SMCI on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
Super Micro Is Down 32% in a Year. Is It Time to Sell, or Load Up? ©Edgar G. Biehle from Getty Images via Canva
Key Takeaways

Super Micro stock is down 32% over the past year after a revenue miss, an export-control indictment of people tied to the company and a $5.6 billion stock sale.

The business has improved: fiscal 2026 sales rose 78% to $39.1 billion, and preliminary September-quarter sales beat its own guidance by about $4 billion.

Growth has come at a cost: free cash flow was negative $7.0 billion in fiscal 2026, and the share count is still rising.

At 7.5x forward earnings, the stock looks too cheap if the Nov. 3 report confirms the early numbers.

Super Micro Computer (SMCI:NASDAQ) stock is down 32% in the past year (through Tuesday's close), even though the company just said its September quarter came in about $4 billion above its own guidance.

Investors got burned three times

It started in November 2025, when fiscal first-quarter sales of $5.0 billion missed guidance of $6 billion to $7 billion.

The December quarter swung the other way: sales hit $12.7 billion, but one data center customer took about 63% of revenue, and gross margin sank to 6.3%.

Then in March, the Justice Department charged three people tied to Super Micro, including a co-founder. Prosecutors say they diverted about $2.5 billion of U.S. AI technology to China. The company wasn't named as a defendant, but the stock lost a third of its value on March 20.

And in June, Super Micro raised $5.6 billion by selling common stock and mandatory convertible preferred. The common went out at $27.50 a share, a year after the company bought back stock at $40.89. (Not great timing.)

Meanwhile, the business got much better

Gross margin climbed from 6.3% in the December quarter to 9.9% in March and 17.5% in June. That quarter, enterprise and channel customers made up half of sales.

Fiscal 2026 sales rose 78% to $39.1 billion, and new orders topped $60 billion. Management guided fiscal 2027 sales to $65 billion to $72 billion.

CEO Charles Liang credits the customer mix: "As demand accelerates, we are improving profitability through a richer enterprise customer mix."

Still, one-time items and deals that slipped into later quarters helped June's margin, so 17.5% isn't the new baseline.

Then came the Oct. 20 update: estimated September-quarter sales of $18.5 billion to $19.5 billion. That's nearly four times the year-ago quarter and well above the $15.23 billion analysts expected. The estimated 12.0% to 12.5% gross margin beat guidance, too.

Palantir Technologies (NASDAQ:PLTR) and Super Micro Computer (NASDAQ:SMCI) are popular artificial intelligence stocks. Since January 2023, Palantir has added 3,000% and Super Micro has advanced 325%. But the Wall Street analysts below think the stocks are overvalued.

Brent Thill at Jefferies recommends selling Palantir. His target price of $80 per share implies 60% downside from its current share price of $199.

Mehdi Hosseini at Susquehanna recommends selling Super Micro. His target price of $15 per share implies 57% downside from the current share price of $35.

Here's what investors should know about these popular AI stocks.

Image source: Getty Images.

Palantir Technologies: 60% downside implied by Jefferies' target price

Palantir develops data analytics and artificial intelligence (AI) platforms to help customers in the public and private sectors integrate data, identify actionable insights, and automate work. Forrester Research recently ranked Palantir as a leader in AI platforms, and Sanjit Singh at Morgan Stanley sees Palantir emerging as the standard in enterprise AI.

The bull case centers around unique software. Whereas traditional analytics tools feature dashboards that tell clients what is happening, Palantir goes further. Its software revolves around a decision-making framework that helps customers decide what should happen next, and it lets them execute actions within the platform.

Palantir is also popular for providing flexibility and supporting privacy. Its AI platform gives customers the freedom to deploy the large language models of their choosing and swap between models without rewriting underlying applications. Palantir's software also includes governance controls that ensure business data is never fed back to model developers.

The bear case for Palantir is entirely focused on its valuation. Despite impressive financial results -- revenue increase 93% in the second quarter, the 12th consecutive acceleration -- Palantir currently trades at 78 times sales, making it the most expensive stock in the S&P 500 by a wide margin. The next closest contender is CrowdStrike at 50 times sales.

Indeed, Brent Thill says Palantir has excellent fundamentals, but the valuation simply does not make sense. He also thinks the company may be underinvesting in future growth, citing its high margins as evidence. But Thill is in the minority on Wall Street, as most analysts think the stock is undervalued. Palantir has a median target price of $223 per share, implying 12% upside from its current share price of $199.

Why is Super Micro (SMCI) stock soaring today
What happened?

Shares of server solutions provider Super Micro (NASDAQ:SMCI) jumped 7.5% in the afternoon session after Reuters reported, citing two people familiar with the matter, that Super Micro-backed cloud computing firm Argentum AI is negotiating a $5 billion financing deal for artificial intelligence chips with a private credit firm. According to the report, the debt financing will fund additional artificial intelligence chips for a data center in Poland secured with DL Invest Group. The hardware is intended to be leased to clients that do not hold investment-grade credit ratings.

The shares closed the day at $35.09, up 7.3% from the previous close.

Is now the time to buy Super Micro? Access our full analysis report here, it's free.

What is the market telling us

Super Micro's shares are extremely volatile and have had 67 moves greater than 5% over the last year. In that context, today's move indicates the market considers this news meaningful but not something that would fundamentally change its perception of the business.

The previous big move we wrote about was 6 days ago when the stock gained 11.1% on the news that the company issued a preliminary business update projecting first-quarter fiscal 2027 revenue between $18.5 billion and $19.5 billion. In a press release, the company raised its sales outlook from prior guidance of $14.5 billion to $15.5 billion, primarily crediting increased demand for AI platforms. That updated range sits well above the $15.23 billion consensus expectation compiled from analysts polled by LSEG, as reported by Reuters. The server maker also lifted its gross margin forecast to between 12.0% and 12.5%, up from prior guidance of 10.4% to 10.8% and the 10.15% LSEG consensus, citing favorable customer and product mix.Simultaneously lifting revenue guidance by $4 billion and projecting wider gross margins indicates that high-density computing demand remains robust and pricing power intact. Forward-looking guidance figures often alter investor valuation models, and establishing defined revenue expectations in advance can drive significant trading activity.

Super Micro is up 13.3% since the beginning of the year, but at $35.08 per share, it is still trading 33.4% below its 52-week high of $52.69 from October 2025. Investors who bought $1,000 worth of Super Micro's shares 5 years ago would now be looking at an investment worth $9,933.

(Updates with market moves at the end of the day, and other changes, if any.)

The Nasdaq Composite and the S&P 500 rose for a second consecutive session Tuesday following the latest set of earnings reports, ahead of the Federal Reserve's decision on interest rates.

The Nasdaq closed 1.2% higher at 26,477.81, while the S&P 500 advanced 0.6% to 7,722.60. The Dow Jones Industrial Average was little changed at 52,377.57. Among sectors, technology paced the gainers, while energy saw the steepest decline.

Pentair (PNR) was the best performer on the S&P 500, up nearly 13%, after the company released its third-quarter results on Tuesday.

Also among the S&P 500's notable gainers were Dell Technologies (DELL) and Super Micro Computer (SMCI).

United Parcel Service (UPS) raised its full-year guidance, saying the outlook for holiday demand is strong. The stock advanced 5.8%.

Boeing (BA) slumped nearly 11%, the worst performer on the Dow and the second-steepest drop on the S&P 500. The US planemaker's third-quarter loss narrowed less than projected as revenue in its commercial airplanes division unexpectedly declined amid a less favorable aircraft delivery mix and higher production and supply-chain costs.

The Federal Open Market Committee kicked off its monetary policy meeting on Tuesday and is widely expected leave its benchmark lending rate unchanged on Wednesday. The anticipated pause would follow a 25-basis-point rate increase in September, the Fed's first hike in just over three years intended to tame inflation.

Most Fed officials expected another rate hike by year-end, though they vowed to base their future policy decisions on fresh data, according to minutes from the central bank's September meeting, which were released earlier this month.

"Of course, even if the Fed opts to hike again in December, a combined 50 (basis-point) increase will most likely prove insufficient to quell price pressures," Stifel said in a note Tuesday. "Again, given the years of elevated costs post-pandemic and the more recent upside risks to costs stemming from the conflict overseas sending energy costs alone up 37% in September from a year ago, it will most assuredly take a firm longer-run commitment and more than a couple of rate increases to tame inflation."

The Fed's terminal interest rate could surpass its 2023-24 peak, especially if the artificial intelligence spending boom continues, TS Lombard said Tuesday.

West Texas Intermediate crude oil was down 1.8% at $99.92 a barrel in Tuesday late-afternoon trade, while Brent dropped 1.6% to $113.98. However, both benchmarks remain on track for their fourth consecutive monthly advance.

Iran's officials met with representatives from Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey on Monday.

"A more sustained decline in prices would likely require credible signals from all sides that tensions are easing, alongside tangible progress towards restoring the free movement of oil and shipping through the Strait of Hormuz," Saxo Bank said in a report Tuesday.

In economic news, US consumer confidence moved higher in October amid a pullback in gasoline prices, The Conference Board said.

Treasury yields were higher, with the two-year rate up 2.4 basis points at 4.74% and the 10-year rate rising 0.9 basis points to 5%.

Spot gold climbed 1.1% to $4,060.87 per troy ounce, while silver edged up 0.3% to $54.49 per ounce.
